claims.text: High-entropy-alloy nanoparticle premelting and melting behavior is jointly governed by alloy composition and nanoparticle size.
Smaller high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles have lower premelting temperatures than larger nanoparticles.
Smaller high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles have lower melting temperatures than larger nanoparticles.
Some high-entropy-alloy compositions have lower premelting and melting temperatures than other compositions.
Reduced nanoparticle size increases surface energy.
Increased surface energy lowers the premelting and melting temperatures of high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
High-entropy alloys possess distinctive chemical and physical complexity.
The chemical and physical complexity of high-entropy alloys contributes to composition-dependent premelting and melting temperatures.
Composition can affect temperature-dependent chemical clustering and short-range ordering in an Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni high-entropy alloy.
A systematic comparison should vary alloy composition and nanoparticle size while measuring premelting and melting temperatures.
The expected observation is a correlation among composition, nanoparticle size, and premelting or melting temperature.
A well-characterized, thermally stable high-entropy-alloy nanoparticle can serve as the baseline.
The hypothesis is intended to apply broadly to high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles across varying compositions and sizes under thermal-stability conditions.
The exact relationship among composition, size, and premelting or melting temperature is currently unknown.
Failure to observe any correlation between composition or size and premelting or melting temperature would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The mechanism identifies increased surface energy as a governing cause, but the falsification rule lists observation of 'surface effects' as a different governing factor that would falsify the hypothesis. Increased surface energy is itself a surface effect, so this proposed falsifier overlaps with the stated mechanism.
